106.title: Gentle with the ledger
106.hook: Seneca reviews his day without hiding anything, then tells himself: see that you don't do it again, this time I forgive you (On Anger 3.36)
106.howItsDone: People who keep a Stoic evening review often follow Seneca's pattern from On Anger 3.36: go over the day honestly, name what went wrong, note what to do next time, and end by letting it go.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Sextius, Seneca's teacher, and his three questions at bedtime. Your line was what did I mend.

Around one in the morning, the replay starts, uninvited. The awkward thing you said at lunch. The email you sent too fast. The thing you should have said to your mother in 2014. For some people, that's what evening review means, and their stomach drops at the words. But it isn't a review. It's a trial with no defense lawyer and no end. If that's you, this story is for you, because Seneca describes his own review, and it has something the 1am trial never has. A pardon.

In the same passage from On Anger, right after Sextius's questions, Seneca tells what he does himself. Each night, when the light is out, he goes over the whole day, and he says he hides nothing from himself and passes over nothing. Why should he fear any of his mistakes, he asks, when he can say to himself, in paraphrase: see that you don't do that again; this time, I forgive you. Then come his examples, and they're wonderfully ordinary. You argued too hotly in that discussion; next time, don't pick a fight with people who don't know better. You warned that man more frankly than you should have, and you didn't help him, you offended him. Next time, think about whether what you say is true, and also whether the person can bear to hear it. Look at the shape. Seneca is honest: he doesn't pretend the argument went fine. He names the fault exactly. He draws a lesson for next time. And he closes the ledger with a pardon. Not a shrug, not an excuse: a forgiveness that comes after the honesty, not instead of it. That's what the 1am trial is missing. It keeps reopening the case because nobody ever rules. Seneca rules. Guilty, lesson noted, forgiven, go to sleep. A review without the forgiveness turns into punishment, and punishment can make people hide from their faults rather than mend them. A review with it makes the next night's honesty easier. Gentleness here isn't softness. It's what lets you keep looking.

107.title: Pythagoras' three questions
107.hook: the Golden Verses: where did I slip, what did I do, what did I leave undone? (Golden Verses 40–44)
107.howItsDone: People drawn to ancient philosophy sometimes use the Golden Verses' three questions as an evening review: where did I go wrong, what did I do, what did I leave undone.

segments.voice: Yesterday Seneca closed his ledger with a pardon: this time, I forgive you. Your line was forgiven this time.

You know Pythagoras from school. The triangle. A squared plus b squared. What school usually leaves out: around 500 BCE, Pythagoras also led a community in southern Italy that was half math club, half spiritual order. His followers kept rules about food, silence and friendship, and believed the soul lives many lives. And they had an evening habit that Sextius and Seneca would inherit, centuries later. It survives in a short old poem, the Golden Verses, and it asks three questions before sleep.
screen: `THE TRIANGLE FROM SCHOOL.` → `HALF MATH CLUB, HALF ORDER.` → `A POEM BEFORE SLEEP.`

segments.voice: The Golden Verses are about seventy lines of advice, credited to Pythagoras but almost certainly written down by his followers much later. Nobody knows exactly when; scholars' guesses range over several centuries. Near the middle comes the evening practice. In paraphrase: don't let sleep close your eyes until you've gone over each thing you did today, three times. Where did I go wrong? What did I do? What that I ought to have done did I leave undone? If you've done badly, the poem says, be troubled by it; if well, be glad. Put these beside Sextius's questions from two days ago and you'll see a family likeness, and one real difference. Sextius asked about improvement: what did I cure, where am I better. The Golden Verses ask something harder to see: what did I leave undone? Most reviews only catch the things you did. The sharp word. The late email. But a day is also made of what you didn't do. The friend you meant to call. The thank-you that stayed in your head. The walk you skipped. Those make no noise, so they never show up at 1am. The third question goes looking for them on purpose. The habit traveled: Epictetus quotes these same lines to his students in the Discourses, and tells them to use the verses in daily life, not just recite them. Three questions, from a community most people remember only for a triangle.

segments.voice: Run the three questions over the last day: find one moment where you slipped, even a little, then one where you did well, and let yourself be glad about it. Then ask slowly, what did I leave undone, and let something quiet surface, a message, a kindness, a small promise. Don't fix it now; just notice it.

108.title: The examen
108.hook: Ignatius of Loyola's nightly review looks for gratitude before faults (Spiritual Exercises 43)
108.howItsDone: Jesuits pray the examen, usually daily, and other Catholics and some Protestants use it too, often in a short form: give thanks, ask for light, review the day, ask forgiveness, and look ahead to tomorrow.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Golden Verses and their third question. Your line was what did I leave undone.

At the siege of Pamplona, a Spanish soldier named Iñigo was hit by a cannonball that shattered his leg. Bored in bed through the long months of recovery, he asked for novels about knights. The house didn't have any. It had a life of Christ and a book of saints. He read them, and something in him turned. He became Ignatius of Loyola, and later founded the Jesuits, a Catholic religious order. He also wrote a little handbook, the Spiritual Exercises, and in it is an evening review that people still pray. Its first step comes before any talk of faults.
screen: `A CANNONBALL AT PAMPLONA.` → `NO NOVELS, ONLY SAINTS.` → `IGNATIUS OF LOYOLA.`

segments.voice: Examen is Latin for an examination. It also meant the needle on a set of scales, the little pointer that shows which way things are tipping: a good picture for a daily look at which way your life is leaning. In the Spiritual Exercises, section 43, Ignatius lays out five points. The first, in paraphrase: give thanks to God for the good things you have received. Only after that: ask for light to see your faults, go over the day hour by hour, ask forgiveness, and resolve to do better tomorrow. Put that beside this week's reviews. Sextius began with what you cured. The Golden Verses began with where you slipped. Ignatius begins with thanks. Before you look for what went wrong, you look for what was given. Why start there? Catholics and other Christians who pray the examen would say it's because the whole review happens in the presence of a loving God, and gratitude puts you where you can see that. You don't have to share that belief to notice what the order does. Start with faults, and the mind tends to stay in the courtroom. Start with what was good today, the coffee, the kind text, the moment the light came through the window, and you meet your faults from somewhere steadier. Today the examen is prayed by Jesuits, by other Catholics, and by some Protestants too, often in a shorter modern form. For those who pray it, it is a prayer, not a technique.

segments.voice: Go back over the last day, and before anything else, find its best moment, even a tiny one, a laugh, a good meal, a text from someone, and stay with it for a few breaths, glad. If you pray, you can give thanks in your own tradition's way. Only then, if something went wrong, look at it gently, from there.

109.title: Franklin's chart
109.hook: Benjamin Franklin tracked thirteen virtues, one a week, with a dot for every slip (Autobiography)
109.howItsDone: Franklin's method from his Autobiography is still copied by some people who keep habit trackers: a short list of virtues, one given close attention each week, with a mark each evening for every slip.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the examen, the evening review Ignatius begins with thanks. Your line was gratitude first.

Before habit apps, before streaks and badges, a young printer in Philadelphia made himself a little book. He ruled each page in red ink: columns for the days of the week, rows for thirteen virtues. Every evening he went down the rows and put a small black dot wherever he'd slipped. That printer was Benjamin Franklin, years before most people knew his name. He tells the story in his Autobiography, and he's funny about it, because it did not go the way he planned.
screen: `A PRINTER IN PHILADELPHIA.` → `RED LINES, THIRTEEN ROWS.` → `A BLACK DOT FOR EVERY SLIP.`

segments.voice: Franklin says he set out, boldly, to arrive at moral perfection. He listed thirteen virtues, each with a short rule. Temperance: don't eat or drink to excess. Silence. Order. Resolution. Frugality. Industry. Sincerity. Justice. Moderation. Cleanliness. Tranquility. Chastity. And humility, which he added later, after a friend told him, kindly, that he was proud. His clever move: he didn't try all thirteen at once. He gave each virtue one week of close attention, while just marking the others, so he got through the list in thirteen weeks, four times a year. How did it go? He was surprised to find himself, in his own words, so much fuller of faults than I had imagined. The dots piled up. Order, keeping his papers and hours in their places, cost him so much effort that he was almost ready to give up on it. He compares himself to a man who wanted his whole axe polished bright, got tired of turning the grinding wheel, and decided he liked a speckled axe best. And yet the ending is gentle. He never reached perfection, he says, but the attempt made him a better and happier man than he would otherwise have been. The chart turns this week's evening review into something you can see, and adds one idea: focus. Not every fault, every night. One virtue, for one week, noticed closely. Small enough to actually do.

110.title: Your two bookends
110.hook: assemble a one-minute morning and a one-minute evening
110.tomorrow: up to us, not up to us
110.howItsDone: Some people who keep a reflective practice hold the day at both ends: a short preview in the morning and a short review at night, drawn from sources like Marcus Aurelius, Seneca, the Golden Verses, the examen or Franklin's chart.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Franklin's chart, thirteen virtues and a dot for every slip. Your line was one virtue a week.

A shelf of books with nothing at either end. They lean, they slide, one falls, and the whole row goes down like dominoes. Put a heavy bookend at each side, and the same books stand straight all week. A day can be like that shelf. It starts with a phone alarm and a scroll, ends with a scroll and a phone alarm, and everything in between slumps. This week brought six ways to hold the ends. Today you choose two, one for each end, and make them yours.
screen: `A SHELF WITH NO ENDS.` → `EVERYTHING SLUMPS.` → `ONE BOOKEND AT EACH SIDE.`

segments.voice: Look back at the week. For the morning: Marcus Aurelius at dawn, in the Meditations. Expect the busy-body and the ungrateful, remember they're your kin, and decide how you'll meet them. Your line was I'll meet them kindly. For the evening, four reviews. Seneca's teacher Sextius: what did I cure, what did I resist, in what am I better? Seneca's own ledger, honest and then closed with a pardon: forgiven this time. The Golden Verses, credited to Pythagoras: where did I slip, what did I do, what did I leave undone? Ignatius of Loyola's examen: gratitude first, then the faults. And Franklin's chart, which added focus: one virtue a week. They don't all agree, and they don't need to. Ignatius prays; Seneca judges himself; Franklin keeps a chart. Each belongs to its own world. What they share is a shape: the day held at both ends, a look forward at the start, a look back at the finish. Here's one way to build yours. Morning, one minute: a preview, like Marcus. Who will I meet, where will it be hard, how do I want to be? Evening, one minute: pick one review. Maybe gratitude first, then one question, what did I mend or what did I leave undone, and end with the pardon. Two minutes a day in total. And like last week's breath routine, the version you'll actually keep beats the perfect one.

111.title: Up to us, not up to us
111.hook: Epictetus opens his Handbook: some things are up to us, some are not (Enchiridion 1)
111.howItsDone: Some people who practice Stoicism sort a worry into what is up to them and what is not, following the first lines of Epictetus's Enchiridion, and put their effort only into the first.

segments.voice: Yesterday you built your bookends, one minute each. Your line was open and close the day.

No say over where you live. No say over what work you do. Not even a say over whether your body belongs to you. The old accounts say Epictetus began life that way: born enslaved, and lame in one leg. Later he was freed, became a teacher, and was banished from Rome with the other philosophers. If anyone had a right to say nothing is up to me, it was him. Instead, he built his whole teaching on the question of what is. A new week: the dichotomy of control.
screen: `BORN ENSLAVED.` → `FREED, TAUGHT, BANISHED.` → `WHAT IS UP TO ME?`

segments.voice: Epictetus didn't write books. His student Arrian took notes, and later boiled the teaching down into a small handbook, the Enchiridion, which means something held in the hand, ready to use. It opens like this, in George Long's 1877 translation: Of things some are in our power, and others are not. The Greek phrase is eph' hēmin: up to us, in our power. Epictetus draws the line sharply. Up to us: our opinions, our impulses, our desires and aversions; in a word, our own acts of mind. Not up to us: our body, our property, our reputation, our office; in a word, whatever is not our own doing. Then comes the promise. Treat as yours only what is yours, and what belongs to others as theirs, and nobody will ever force you or hinder you, and you won't blame anyone. Notice how short the first list is. Not the weather, not the traffic, not what your boss decides, not even how your body feels today. Only how you judge and how you respond. That sounds like bad news, and at first it is. But it's also where the relief is. A lot of worry goes into pushing on the second list: replaying what someone thinks, straining at what's already happened. Epictetus says that door doesn't open from your side. Put your hand on the one that does. Two columns, mine and not mine: a sorting a worried mind can do in one breath.

segments.voice: Let two or three worries come up, and take one. Ask which part is yours, your judgment, your effort, your response, and which is not, what others decide, what's already done, what happens next. Picture each part going into its column, then rest your attention on the mine column.

112.title: The archer
112.hook: Cicero's Stoic: the archer does everything to aim well, and hitting the mark isn't wholly his (On Ends 3.22)
112.howItsDone: People who draw on Stoicism often use Cicero's archer when facing an uncertain outcome: they judge themselves by the quality of their effort and hold the result lightly.

segments.voice: Yesterday: eph' hēmin, up to us, from Epictetus's Handbook. Your line was mine or not mine.

You spent a week on the job application. You rewrote the cover letter four times. You prepared for the interview. You were kind to the receptionist. And they gave the job to the manager's nephew. Did you fail? Most people would say yes, because they score themselves on the result. But yesterday's line raises a hard question. If the result was never fully in your hands, what exactly were you supposed to succeed at? The Stoics had a picture for the answer, and a Roman writer saved it.
screen: `A WEEK ON THE APPLICATION.` → `THE MANAGER'S NEPHEW.` → `DID YOU FAIL?`

segments.voice: It comes from Cicero, in On Ends, a book about what the goal of life is. Cicero wasn't a Stoic himself, but in the third book he lets a Stoic speak: Cato the Younger, famous for his stubborn honesty. Cato says, in paraphrase: imagine someone whose job is to aim a spear or an arrow at a target. Everything he can do, he must do, to aim straight. Choose the bow, set the feet, draw, breathe, release clean. That is his goal, the thing he truly works for. Hitting the mark, he says, is something to be chosen, but not desired in the same way. Why? Once the arrow leaves the string, it belongs to the wind. A gust, a bird, a target that moves. The archer can do everything right and miss, or do it badly and hit by luck. So the Stoics moved the scoreboard: your success is the shot, not the landing. Aim with everything you have. Then let go, twice: once with your fingers, and once with your heart. That doesn't mean not caring where the arrow lands. Cato still wants to hit. It means your worth, and your peace, don't ride on the arrow. Back to the application. You aimed well: the rewrites, the preparation, the kindness to the receptionist. That part was yours, and you did it. The nephew was wind. Tomorrow you can aim again, and you'll aim better for having practiced.
screen: `CATO SPEAKS IN CICERO'S BOOK.` · `DO EVERYTHING TO AIM STRAIGHT.` · `THE ARROW BELONGS TO THE WIND.` · `SUCCESS IS THE SHOT.` · then, large: `AIM, THEN LET GO.`

segments.voice: Think of one thing you're working on where the result isn't yours to decide: a test, an offer, a hard conversation, someone's recovery. On the in-breath, picture drawing the bow with all your care and effort; on the out-breath, the release, the arrow gone, the result handed over. Draw and release a few times, then just breathe.
The archer. Do everything to aim well; once the arrow flies, hitting the mark is not wholly yours. Today's word.
Your line: aim, then let go. The shot is yours; the wind isn't. One hundred twelve days in.
